subject: Stop the difficulty slider overflowing its own label
body:
The site auditor caught it on the money guide at every one of five viewports,
always by exactly two pixels: 360 in a 358 box, 450 in a 448 box. A constant
overflow that does not scale with the viewport is not a width problem.

A range input carries a default horizontal margin of about 2px, so inline-size
100% makes it exactly that much wider than the label wrapping it. Zeroing the
margin fixes every width at once.

The auditor now covers the money guide, the search page and a file page too, so
the three new surfaces are held to the same 55-combination standard as the rest.

subject: No redirects, a master search on every page, and a money guide
body:
Four things, and the first turned out to be the largest.

**No redirects.** The source sends you elsewhere in three ways and each left a
hole here. 1,970 internal links across the corpus went nowhere and rendered as
plain text; 16 do now, and those sixteen are the source wiki's own machinery —
What-links-here queries, an upload form, contributor pages — which genuinely has
no equivalent in a static archive and says so rather than pretending.

  885 Category: links -> the category pages that already existed
  891 File: links    -> 836 new file pages, 827 with the archived image
  178 Template: Nav  -> the category each navigation box was pointing at
   83 alternate names -> a page of their own, content and all

An alternate name was previously followed at link-rewrite time, which made the
name unreachable: click "Blue pine", arrive at "Blue Pine", and nothing recorded
that the name you asked for existed. Each is a real page now with a canonical
link to the primary article — the right tool where an HTTP redirect is not.

That exposed the case-collision fault again. 20 alternate names differ from a
real article only in capitalisation, and on this filesystem "Blue_pine" and
"Blue_Pine" are one directory, so the second write silently replaces the first.
Exactly what once made the build report 1,063 articles while writing 1,059.
Aliases now share the articles' disambiguation, numbered after them so no
existing URL moves, and a guard proves no two of 1,146 entries share a slug.

**Master search.** A plain GET form in the top bar of all 2,053 pages,
deliberately not scripted: a thousand article pages never hydrate, so a search
needing JavaScript would be decoration on most of the site. Enter reaches
/search/, which holds one index over every article, alias, category, file and
standing page — 2,053 entries, 119KB gzipped, fetched only there.

**Money guide.** 144 items from 446 sell-side prices, ranked by earnings and by
difficulty computed independently — difficulty never reads price, because scoring
effort from value and then ranking by value is circular and makes "worth a lot,
easy to reach" impossible to express. Which is the guide's best finding:
Magnetite, $600 a stud, starting island, difficulty 1.5.

Three defects caught while building it, each of which would have shipped a
confidently wrong guide:

  - The generic Price field is what a thing COSTS. 398 items carrying it also
    carry a Shop or Cost field. Reading those as income put a $10,000,000
    shop-bought warhead — the biggest money sink in the game — at number one.
  - The unit comes from the value, never the field name. A beehive's "Log" is a
    flat $1389, not per stud; trusting the label put it thirty times above every
    real per-stud price. Per-stud and per-item are now separate tables.
  - The event-currency filter caught U+2745 and missed U+2744, so a log priced
    1 snowflake per stud was read as one dollar.

Hardness is deliberately unused: 22 of the 34 articles carrying it record "?".

subject: Bring the in-app changelog up to the current history
body:
Generated from git log at build time, so it can never contain the commit that
carries it — it is always exactly one behind, by construction. This lands the
session's work in the changelog viewer; the next build will show a one-commit
diff again, which is expected rather than a defect to chase.

subject: Refresh the reference and differentiation captures after the layout fixes
body:
The nine reference screens and the four differentiation captures predated the
vendored fonts, the docs-nav column fix and the heading break rule, so they were
pictures of a build that no longer exists — which is worse than no reference,
because a comparison against one reads as a pass.

Recaptured from the deployed build at e2beb9c under the same pinned tuples, and
the digests in the parity inventory updated to match. Accessibility evidence
refreshed alongside: 40 surface/viewport combinations, all six checks at zero.

subject: Let a heading break when a single word cannot fit its column
body:
At 320px the word "Documentation," measured 295px in a 288px box, and
overflow-wrap: normal has no break opportunity inside a word — so the tail was
simply cut off. Nothing failed; the heading just quietly lost its last letters on
the narrowest phones.

break-word rather than anywhere: it breaks only when a word genuinely cannot fit,
so ordinary headings still wrap at spaces and read normally. Applied at the
heading reset instead of the one page that showed it, because any long word in
any heading has the same problem and the next one would not be noticed either.

subject: Fix the docs nav overflowing its column after the font change
body:
The site auditor caught it on the deployed build: /docs/ overflowed the body at
320px and the nav overflowed its own box at every desktop width. Every child of
the aside measured exactly 318px inside a 288px column, which rules out the usual
suspect — an unbreakable string would have made one child wide, not all of them.

The cause was the container. A single-column grid sizes its implicit column to
max-content, so the widest child decides the width and the 18rem track is only a
suggestion. The search field is the widest thing in there because an <input>
carries an intrinsic size, and it pushed the aside 30px past its column.
minmax(0, 1fr) makes the column shrinkable, which plain 1fr does not.

Vendoring Inter did not create this; it revealed it. The previous fallback face
was narrow enough to fit by luck, so the layout was one font substitution away
from breaking on any visitor who did not happen to have that face installed.

Handoff refreshed against the tree: 34 of 34 inventory rows, what is still not
done, and the traps this pass cost time on.

subject: Close the last three inventory rows, vendor the fonts, hash the reserved list
body:
Finishes the verification pass: the completeness inventory now stands at 34 of 34
rows built, each naming its implementation, documentation and evidence.

Design parity and source differentiation (F-015, F-032). Nine reference screens
captured from the deployed site under pinned tuples and digest-locked, plus nine
differentiation rows, each naming what the source wiki does, the counter-treatment
here, and the paired capture that shows it at one identical tuple. check-parity
fails when a row loses its evidence, so a claim cannot outlive the picture backing
it. Eight mutations prove it red, the unmutated inventories prove it green.

Accessibility (F-031). 40 surface/viewport combinations measured on the built site:
no horizontal overflow, no unnamed controls, no missing alt text, exactly one h1
per page, no target under 24px, nothing overflowing its own box. The completeness
guard immediately caught the docs path in that row pointing at a file that did not
exist yet, which is the whole reason rows name artefacts instead of describing them.

Fonts. The token stack named Inter and JetBrains Mono and shipped neither, so how
the site rendered depended on what each visitor happened to have installed. Both
are now vendored: every weight and every unicode-range subset the upstream returns,
13 files, 278KB, font-weight and unicode-range copied verbatim so no axis is claimed
that the binary lacks. check-fonts refuses a missing file, a drifted digest, a
collapsed weight range, a remote url(), or a stack naming a family nobody vendored.

Reserved-phrase check. The wiki guard listed the phrases it refuses in plaintext,
so the leak-preventing check was itself publishing them. The list is one-way now:
63 digests, hits reported by digest, nothing readable committed. Two defects found
while proving it — the digest and the scanner each had their own copy of the
tokenizer and silently disagreed, and splitting hyphens manufactured a two-word run
from a URL slug that failed all 1,130 pages on a phrase none of them contained.
Both fixed; the guard is proved red on an injected phrase and green once removed.

Renamed --ok-cat-* to --ok-category-* so "category" stops reading as something else
in every future scan.

ROADMAP reconciled against the tree rather than edited around it. Items that
changed approach are recorded with the reason instead of being ticked: media ships
as committed display-size WebP rather than release volumes, one width rather than
three, and the design references are captured from the built site rather than
authored ahead of it. The screen recording is still not done and stays unticked.

subject: Give the grid item a zero minimum too, not just the flex items inside it
body:
The previous fix set min-width on the row and its name and changed nothing,
because the <li> between them is a GRID item, and a grid item's default
min-width is `auto` exactly like a flex item's. Two levels down was shrinking;
the level in the middle was not. Measured again rather than assumed fixed --
which is the only reason this was caught instead of shipped.

subject: Let browse rows shrink, and stop the auditor measuring a stale build
body:
A flex item's default min-width is `auto`, which refuses to shrink below its
content. The article name in a browse row would not give way to the thumbnail
and the meta beside it, so the list sat 6px wider than a 320px screen.

The auditor was also lying, in the most expensive direction: it reported the
previous run's defects as still present after they were fixed. Network cache was
disabled, but that covers the browser's own cache and not an edge serving stale
HTML -- and stale HTML points at the previous CSS hash, so every measurement came
from a build that was no longer deployed. Ten minutes went into re-diagnosing
defects that had been fixed an hour earlier. Each run now cache-busts, and the
same fixes measured clean immediately.

subject: Fix the 320px overflow at its actual cause, and give small controls real targets
body:
The floating toolbar was innocent. A paragraph on the About page carried an
unbreakable 24-character snapshot id and overflowed its own box by 82px; that
widened the document, and every fixed element positioned from the right got
pushed out with it. The offender scan compared right edges, so it confidently
named the toolbar -- the element that had been pushed, not the one doing the
pushing.

`overflow-wrap: break-word` was not enough, because a commit SHA or a snapshot id
has no break opportunity at all. It is `anywhere` now, on code and on prose.

The audit gained the check that would have found it in one pass: scan
scrollWidth against clientWidth, not just right edges. An element can overflow
its own box while its right edge sits comfortably inside the viewport, and that
is precisely the case that misdirects.

Two real target-size defects fixed rather than excused. Table sort buttons were a
19px line box; they now carry a full target with the padding inside the cell, so
the table's density is unchanged. The logic lab's ports, remove buttons and
article links were around 20px, which is fine with a mouse and not with a thumb.

subject: Stop the chrome bar pushing the page sideways at 320px
body:
Six floating tool chips measure 498px. At a 320px viewport that is 178px wider
than the screen, and it pushed the whole page sideways -- the one layout rule
this project states outright. Found by measuring the built site at five
viewports, not by looking at it: the bar sits over the content, so nothing looks
obviously wrong until you notice the page scrolls.

Below the breakpoint the tools now collapse behind one control, and the bar is
capped at the viewport width regardless.

The audit itself needed a correction in the other direction. It flagged forty
combinations for "small targets" that were inline links inside paragraphs --
"CC BY-SA 4.0" at 80x19 in a sentence. The target-size rule explicitly exempts
those, because enlarging a link inside a line of text breaks the line box it sits
in. The exemption is now narrow: genuinely inline links in flowing text only,
never a standalone control that happens to be small. A guard that cries wolf
forty times is a guard nobody reads on the forty-first.

subject: Add offline docs, a changelog with commit links, and an honest status surface
body:
Twelve documentation articles, one per feature, each covering what it does, how
it is configured, how it fails, what it deliberately does not claim, and how it
was verified. Every article ends with suggested reading, so nobody is dropped at
a dead end. All of it is bundled into the build, so it works with the network
unplugged, and article-to-article links resolve inside the page rather than
opening a browser or going nowhere.

The changelog is generated from real git history, and every entry carries the
full commit SHA. An entry that says what changed but not where is unverifiable: a
reader who doubts it has no route from the sentence to the code. A wrong SHA is
worse than none, because it sends them somewhere confidently irrelevant, so the
generator proves every referenced commit exists before writing anything and
fails the build rather than emitting a dead link.

Only the English half of each bilingual commit body is carried across. The viewer
renders its own language modes, so shipping both halves would double every entry.

The status surface states what this build is and is not, including that audio and
video are not archived and that CI runs no tests by policy. Anything unfinished
says so there rather than being left for somebody to discover.

Both generators run in prebuild, because documentation and a changelog generated
"whenever somebody last ran the script" are exactly as stale as they sound.

subject: Add scheduled settings and a local file converter
body:
A schedule rule takes a date range, a time window, every day or chosen weekdays,
and overlays settings while it matches. The semantics are decided rather than
left to whatever the code happened to do: times are in the visitor's own
timezone and it is named on the surface; a window crossing midnight is two
intervals rather than an empty one; equal start and end means the whole day,
because nobody typing the same time twice meant a zero-length window; and when
several rules match the LAST enabled one wins, which the surface states instead
of leaving precedence to an array order nobody can see.

A schedule is an overlay, never a write. Turning every rule off returns exactly
what was there before, because the base settings were never overwritten to begin
with.

The matching logic lives in lib rather than the component, so every boundary is
driven without a clock -- which is the only practical way to test a
midnight-crossing window. Twelve assertions cover the crossing, inclusive start
and exclusive end, the whole-day case, weekdays, date bounds, a disabled rule,
malformed input refused rather than coerced into an accidental match, and
deterministic precedence.

The converter runs entirely in this browser, and that constraint decides the
catalogue rather than being hidden by it. Nine conversions work: JSON, CSV, TSV
and Markdown between each other, images re-encoded through a canvas, text
normalised, anything to base64. Seven more are LISTED AND DISABLED with the exact
reason -- PDF split, merge and text extraction need a bundled library this page
does not ship; ZIP needs central-directory parsing the browser does not expose;
HEIC cannot be decoded here at all. Hiding those makes the catalogue look
complete and sends somebody hunting for a converter that was never there.

Every lossy conversion says what it costs before it runs: JPEG has no
transparency, WebP flattens the colour profile, CSV keeps no types, and only the
first frame of an animation is drawn.

subject: Add append-only history, exports in eight formats, and a local authenticator
body:
History records what CHANGED, not that something did: "accent: #ffab5e →
#7fb2ff", never "Updated". An unchanged save records nothing, so the panel stays
a list of real events rather than a log of saves.

Restoring is itself a NEW entry, never a rewrite. An undo can therefore be undone
and that undo undone in turn. A restore that discards the branch it replaces is
the one failure that makes a history panel unsafe to open, because you cannot
experiment without risking the state you started from.

The action filter is derived from the entries themselves rather than hard-coded,
so a new kind of action appears there automatically instead of being missing from
a list nobody remembered to update. Date range, action and regex search all
compose; none overrides another. Select-all states its scope -- "all 12 matching"
and "all 340 entries" are different buttons, because leaving "all" to mean
whichever the reader assumed is how a bulk action surprises somebody.

Exports cover eight formats that can carry a flat row set faithfully. A history
write never fails the operation it was recording.

The authenticator draws its pairing QR IN THIS PROCESS. Never a QR web service or
a remote chart API: rendering a pairing secret through somebody else's server
hands them the secret on the way to drawing it. The code is true black on white
in both themes, because tinting a QR into the palette is how a scannable code
stops scanning.

Pairing is confirmed with a live code before the entry is saved. Without that
step a mistyped secret locks somebody out of a thing they just set up, and they
find out when they need it. Clock skew against the server is reported plainly,
because codes come from the system clock and a skewed one produces confidently
wrong digits with nothing to read.

subject: Add a logic lab: build circuits from the parts the wiki documents, and run them
body:
The Logic category describes 44 real components -- AND, OR, NOT, XOR and XAND
gates, memory cells, incrementors, clocks, seven-segment displays. An article can
tell you what a XAND gate does. It cannot let you wire four of them into a half
adder and watch the carry appear. That is the gap.

Every part in the palette is one the wiki documents, and each links back to its
article. Three starter circuits ship because a blank canvas is a hard place to
begin: a half adder, a clock driving a counter into a seven-segment display, and
a set/reset latch. They are real working circuits built only from the palette, so
opening one and taking it apart is the tutorial.

The engine evaluates by bounded relaxation rather than a topological sort,
because a real circuit may contain a feedback loop and a topological sort simply
refuses to order one. Sequential parts read the previous tick and write the next,
which is what lets a loop settle at all; a loop that never settles costs a fixed
number of passes and reports itself instead of hanging the tab.

Small decisions that are stated rather than left to chance: an unconnected input
reads 0, so one missing wire cannot make NaN reachable; an input takes one wire
and a second replaces the first, so a value never depends on iteration order;
reset wins a tie in the memory cell, because an ambiguous latch is worse than a
rule somebody can look up.

The engine is pure and tested without a browser -- four full truth tables, NOT,
Greater Than comparing values rather than truthiness, the half adder checked
against real arithmetic, the latch's tie-break, a 13 round-tripping through four
bit lines, and every seven-segment digit lighting the right number of segments.
Proved by breaking XOR into OR and flipping the latch's tie-break: both go red,
both restore green.

subject: Add toy locks on any element, the unlock ladder, and Support Tickets
body:
Right-click anything to lock it, with six policies from a bare PIN to
password-plus-PIN-plus-code. Each lock carries its own policy and its own
credentials: there is no master credential and no inheritance, so unlocking one
element never unlocks another. Passwords are verified against a SHA-256 hash;
nothing is stored in the clear, and a wrong attempt never characterises the
stored value -- not its length, not its composition, not how close it was.

A locked element is genuinely inert. Interception runs at the document level in
the capture phase, so a keyboard press or a programmatic click cannot walk around
a disabled attribute the way it usually can. The keypad and manual entry feed one
validator and one attempt budget, because two routes that disagree are a bug
waiting for whichever one nobody tested.

The unlock ladder replaces a countdown with something to do: dim sum, then ten
sums, then whack-a-mole, then the clock. Falling to the bottom leaves you exactly
where you started, so it can only improve a locked-out afternoon.

Four rules make it safe rather than merely clever, and all four are enforced:
it clears the WAITING and never the credential; it never refunds the attempt
budget; it is capped at three skipped waits per rolling hour, because four
choices is one-in-four and a mole schedule is arithmetic, so without the cap a
script plays past every lockout and brute force gets cheaper; and it never slows
the exponential escalation it skips. A mole hit counts only against a mole
genuinely visible in that cell, once, and the round cannot be won faster than it
lasts.

Under School mode the dim-sum rung is ABSENT rather than skipped with a message,
because a message naming the hidden thing is exactly what School mode forbids.
One function decides the first rung so no surface can get that wrong locally.

TOTP is checked against the three published RFC 6238 SHA-1 vectors, because an
authenticator that is subtly wrong produces codes rejected everywhere with no
error to read.

Support Tickets is the recovery route dressed as a service desk: a ticket number,
a severity nobody will honour, a canned reply of real gravity, and then the only
thing that actually works -- clearing this site's storage. One plain line, outside
the comedy, states that nothing is sent anywhere and nobody is reading it, so no
one sits waiting for a reply that was never coming.

subject: Add the tab strip: docking, pinning, groups, four searches, bulk closes
body:
Docks to any edge and defaults to left, because a screen is wider than it is tall
and a tab label is wider than it is high -- a vertical strip shows more tabs
legibly than the horizontal one every browser trained everyone to expect.

Orientation is not decoration. A vertical strip is aria-orientation="vertical"
and its arrow keys are up and down. Get that wrong and the strip looks perfectly
correct while being unusable by keyboard, which no screenshot will ever reveal.
Labels stay horizontal at every dock: a sideways word is a word nobody reads.

All four tab searches, each with its own field, its own regex builder and its own
state -- this strip, inside one group, groups by name, and every open tab. Two
fields never share a query.

Move-into-group is a picker, not inlined menu items. One menu entry per group is
clutter that grows without bound, so the menu carries a single entry that opens
an anchored picker with its own search and a create-new path.

Both bulk closes share one predicate, so the inverse genuinely negates the same
match rather than reimplementing it with slightly different casing. Neither runs
on an empty query or an invalid pattern; both show the exact count and a preview
first; pinned tabs are excluded by default and NAMED when excluded, because
silently skipping them is indistinguishable from losing them.

subject: Add comparison tables: 17 sortable views the source wiki cannot produce
body:
Every ore's price beside every other ore's, every axe's swing power beside the
rest. The source keeps these facts inside each article's own template, so nobody
reading it can line them up; typed extraction turns that into a grouping problem
and this is the payoff. 349 objects, 84 woods, 54 buildings, 49 ores, 38 axes.

Columns are the fields at least a quarter of that type's articles actually carry.
A column present on three of ninety rows is not a column, it is eighty-seven
empty cells. Fields named `title` are excluded because they just repeat the
article name, which is a duplicate rather than a fact to compare.

Sorting is numeric where a column really is numeric -- $32/stud sorts after
$10/stud rather than before it, which alphabetical order gets wrong every time.
A missing value renders an em dash rather than a blank cell, because a gap in the
source and a gap in the import should not look identical.

subject: Add the chrome every page carries: settings, palette, notifications, attention
body:
Language modes (English, Cantonese, bilingual), both per-language funny sliders
at 5 by default, the dialog emoji switch, appearance with a continuous colour
picker and contrast readout, five independently switchable attention modes, a
narrator with a voice picker per language, and a command palette on Ctrl+Shift+F.

The architecture is the interesting part. Article pages prerender their body as
static HTML that React never owns, so the chrome mounts into its own empty
container instead of hydrating the page. That means all 1,129 surfaces get
working settings, palette and notifications -- not just the handful that happen
to be interactive -- while a thousand article bodies are never re-rendered by a
bundle to produce markup they already have.

Details that are easy to get wrong and are handled deliberately:

Voice enumeration returns nothing on the first call and fills in later behind an
event, so a picker that reads it once reports "no voices installed" on a machine
with forty and looks broken rather than slow. A chosen voice that is not
installed falls back and SAYS SO, keeping the choice rather than silently
resetting it.

The narrator serializes: one utterance at a time, and a superseded line in the
same category replaces the queued one instead of stacking. Errors are exempt from
the rate limit, because a failure nobody heard is the one case where staying
quiet is the wrong behaviour.

Attention modes state facts and nothing else. No streak, no score, no
congratulation, no scolding -- "open for 40 minutes" is the whole feature. They
are named for what they do, so using one discloses nothing to a colleague reading
over your shoulder.

Palette rows are rich: a setting result renders its live control inline, wired to
the same state the settings panel writes. Somebody who can see a value has
usually come to change it.

subject: Show the new design in the README with measured captures
body:
Real captures from the live site at a phone viewport, with the numbers taken from
the running page rather than claimed: no horizontal overflow at 390px, 60 of 63
categories carrying real art, 885 of 1,063 articles, and the browse filters
narrowing 1,063 rows to 87 on "C".

That last one matters more than it reads. A filter that looks like a filter and
does nothing is the decorative-control defect these rules forbid everywhere else,
and the only way to tell the difference is to click it and count what is left.

subject: Push the theme control back to the edge on phones, and tighten the hero
body:
Below the breakpoint the primary nav moves to the bottom bar. The `auto` margin
that separated the wordmark from the theme control lived on that nav, so hiding
it left the control jammed against the title -- correct on a desktop, wrong on
the device most people arrive with. Found in a phone capture, not in the diff.

subject: Archive 2,397 images, and fix the lookup that hid a third of them
body:
Every referenced still image is now archived at display size: WebP, about 25 KB
each, 46 MB in total. The originals average half a megabyte and total roughly
1.6 GB -- one is 8.4 MB for a single map screenshot -- so shipping those would
have undone the reason this site exists. The source's own thumbnailer does the
work.

885 of 1,063 articles carry art, and 60 of 63 categories. It was 520 an hour ago,
and the difference was a lookup: the manifest is keyed by the API's page title,
which uses spaces, while an article's image list uses underscores. MediaWiki
treats those as the same title; a plain object lookup does not. 371 articles were
quietly artless while the manifest, the fetch and the component were all correct.

Two importer defects worth naming. The existence check called readdir() once per
image, which is O(n^2) and degrades as it runs -- 252 images took 25 minutes and
the rate was still falling, and none of it was the network. Reading the directory
once and adding bounded concurrency took it to about 110 a minute. Five images
still fail honestly: two animated GIFs exceed the size cap and three no longer
exist upstream. Those render a placeholder naming the file, because a gap in the
archive and a fault in the site should not look the same.

Also lands build.bat and download-dependencies.bat (both with /s, fetching their
own dependencies), the line counter with per-surviving-line attribution, and a
release workflow that verifies the published release rather than assuming it.

subject: Replace the design: dark-first, image-forward, and a real browse surface
body:
A completely new visual system at the owner's direction. The editorial book-like
version was legible but read as a document; this reads as software. Dark by
default with a light theme, a variable sans throughout instead of a display
serif, generous radii, depth from one soft ambient shadow rather than a stack of
tonal greys, and image-forward tiles where there were text rows.

What survives from v1 is what was actually right: a capped reading measure, real
type hierarchy, colour that carries meaning rather than decorating, and category
identity taken from the game's own material tones.

The theme control is deliberately not a React component. Article pages ship no
JavaScript bundle at all, so a React-driven toggle would render there as a button
that does nothing -- the decorative-control defect these rules forbid. It is about
a kilobyte of inline script instead, applied before first paint so a returning
visitor never sees the wrong theme flash, and it works on all 1,129 pages.

More categorisation, as asked: a /browse/ surface over every article with
first-letter, category and item-type filters that compose with each other and
with the regex search, and category tiles that carry an image. Images are being
fetched at a display size -- the source's own thumbnailer returns WebP at about
25 KB against originals averaging half a megabyte, one of which is 8.4 MB for a
single screenshot.

subject: Make the 1,063 articles reachable: 63 category pages with a real regex builder
body:
Until now the archive had every article and no way to reach one. Sixty-three
category pages are built from the categories articles actually carry -- not a
curated list, so a category cannot quietly lose members -- and the home page's
cards are links rather than decoration.

Each category carries its own search field with its own anchored regex builder:
plain text by default, regex an explicit opt-in, with insertable constructs for
anchors, classes, quantifiers, groups and lookaround, and the four flags. Each
field owns its query, pattern, flags and validation; two fields never share
state. Patterns compile in the visitor's own browser and an unsupported
construct is reported as the engine's own error rather than silently ignored,
because a builder that advertises constructs its engine will not run is worse
than no builder.

Category pages hydrate because a search box is real interaction. Article pages
still ship no script at all -- they are static text, and sending 200 KB of
JavaScript to re-render markup that is already correct is pure cost, a thousand
times over.

subject: Stop a blanket paragraph reset from silently collapsing every article gap
body:
`.ok-prose p { margin: 0 }` has specificity (0,1,1). The spacing rules that give
an article its rhythm are `> * + *`, which is (0,1,0). So the reset won every
time, every paragraph gap measured exactly 0px, and both rules looked entirely
correct in the stylesheet -- the losing one especially.

Measured on the built page rather than read: gaps of [0, 0, 0, 82, 0]. Reading
CSS cannot tell you which rule won; only the running page can.

Paragraph margins are now reset once at the element layer, where "no generic
HTML" belongs, and the spacing rules are left to do the spacing. `p`, `h5` and
`h6` join the required-element list so they keep their own rules.

subject: Unwrap the source's parser div so article paragraphs actually breathe
body:
The reader spaces an article with `.ok-article__body > * + *`. Every paragraph
sat inside the source's single mw-parser-output wrapper, so that selector matched
exactly one element and every article rendered as a wall of text -- with CSS that
reads as entirely correct, which is the hardest kind of layout bug to spot in a
diff and the easiest to spot on a phone. Found by looking at a real capture,
which is the only place it was visible.

Empty paragraphs holding nothing but a line break go too. They are the source's
own spacing hack and here they render as an unexplained gap, because this layout
does its own spacing.

subject: Render all 1,063 articles, and fix four that were quietly overwriting each other
body: Every captured article now has a prerendered page with a Key facts card, a table of contents, resolved internal links and real attribution -- revision, last editor, timestamp and licence. 802 of them carry typed facts pulled from the wikitext, where an infobox is a template call with named parameters and is exact, while the body comes from expanded HTML because re-implementing MediaWiki's template expander is a project of its own. Three defects worth naming, all found by guards rather than by looking: The infobox template list was invented from plausible names and matched 184 of 1,063 articles. This wiki's largest infobox is called Objects, which nothing predicted. Rebuilt from the corpus: 802. Guessing a vocabulary is how a feature ships looking finished while covering a sixth of the data. The CDN survived the sanitiser through

subject: Style every element the site can emit, and guard it with a hand-written list
body:
No generic HTML anywhere. 65 elements get a deliberate treatment, from <sup> and
<abbr> through <table>, <details>, <input type="range"> and <meter>.

This matters more here than on a normal site because most of those elements never
appear in hand-written markup at all -- they arrive inside imported wiki HTML. An
unstyled <blockquote> on one article out of a thousand reads to a visitor exactly
like the stylesheet failed to load, and nobody previews a thousand articles.

Eleven elements are deliberately left to inherit, each with its reason recorded
rather than quietly skipped. <tbody> is the interesting one: it is a row-grouping
box with no appearance of its own, its rows carry the striping and its cells carry
the borders, so a rule on it would be a no-op written purely to satisfy a check.
An honest exemption beats a decorative rule.

The guard checks reality against a hand-written list, not the list against
reality, and it demands a bare type selector. On its first run it refused <thead>
and <tbody> because they only had descendant rules like `thead th` -- a rule about
a child is not a rule about the element, which is precisely what an existence
check usually gets wrong. <thead> then earned a real one: it sticks, so a long
comparison table can be scrolled without losing the header.

subject: Record phase 1 evidence, the handoff, and two traps worth not rediscovering
body:
Real captures from the live site at a 390x844 phone viewport, with the numbers
measured rather than asserted: 18px body at 30.6px leading, no horizontal
overflow, 56px category cards, 55px nav targets.

The full-page capture shows the bottom bar apparently floating mid-page. It is
not a defect, and that was checked rather than waved away -- captureBeyondViewport
renders a sticky element at its stuck viewport position, so in a tall capture it
lands in the middle of the image and looks exactly like a bug. In the real
viewport it sits flush at the bottom and covers nothing. The README says so next
to the picture, because otherwise the next reader files it.

The handoff carries the traps that cost time here: undici being refused the
robots file while the API answers it fine, the bundle guard once validating a
stale dist after a failed build, and a scripted edit that reported no match and
was nearly missed because the syntax check still passed. That last one left the
importer exiting 0 with no output and no corpus, which is the expensive kind of
failure -- everything looks fine and nothing happened.

subject: Capture the whole wiki and make the pages quote only numbers the corpus backs
body:
1,063 articles, 90 redirects and 98 categories are now on disk with their
revision ids, timestamps and last editors, so attribution has something real to
attach to later. The robots verdict recorded with the capture is a plain allow
via the wildcard group.

The counts needed care. The source's own statistics say 1,066 articles; allpages
non-redirects says 1,063. Both are true and they are not the same question, so
the site now shows what it actually holds, names the source's own figure beside
it, and says why they differ instead of quietly picking whichever sounds better.

The bundle guard grew a staleness check, and it went red on a real stale dist
within seconds of being written. A failed vite build leaves the previous output
sitting there, so every assertion passed against an artifact that no longer
matched the tree -- a green run describing a build that had already failed. That
is the worst possible direction for a guard to be wrong in.

subject: Add the completeness guard and importer, and stop using fetch for the source
body:
The build referenced a completeness guard that did not exist, so the deploy fell
over on a missing module. Here it is, and it earned its keep in the first run by
catching a docs file the inventory promised and nobody had written.

The inventory is hand-written and stays that way. A guard that finds features by
scanning the tree can only validate the features already there, so it reports a
clean run on a project missing every one of them -- it never looked, so it never
failed. Six deliberate mutations prove this one bites, including the two that
matter most: a built row whose file is gone, and a built row that quietly names
no implementation at all.

The importer uses node:https rather than the global fetch, and the reason is
written down because the symptom points the wrong way. With an identical user
agent, undici gets HTTP 403 on this source's robots.txt while node:https and curl
both get 200 -- and undici is refused the *policy file* while being served the API
perfectly happily. So a fetch-based importer concludes it is blocked by a source
that explicitly allows exactly what it wants, and the tempting next move is a
--skip-robots flag: the wrong fix to a misread problem. There is no such flag and
there will not be one. The live verdict is a plain allow.

subject: Stand up the Oaklands reader site with a reading-first design system
body:
The source wiki has good content trapped behind a front page of giant image
buttons, infoboxes that fall off the side of a phone, and a heading style that
puts a picture of a dollar sign inside the word "Selling". So: a new site whose
entire design brief is "let someone actually read this".

Material Design 3 is deliberately not used. It is app chrome, and it argues with
long-form reading. Oaklands Reader replaces it: typography carries the structure,
the prose column is capped near 70 characters, chrome gets out of the way, and
category colours come from real material tones instead of being decided by vibes.
The deviation is dated and reasoned in docs/standards/design-language.md rather
than left as a mystery for whoever reads this next.

This phase ships the hosted site and nothing it cannot back up. The category
counts are freshly captured from the live API and real; the articles behind them
are not imported yet, and the front page says so in plain words instead of
implying a finished encyclopedia.

Guards assert the built output rather than the config that produced it, because a
green build only proves a file got written. Every assertion was broken on purpose
and watched go red before being trusted. One of them stayed smugly green while
its own defect sat in front of it -- a token declared mid-line slipped past a
line-start anchor -- and that is exactly why they get broken first.
